We have three distinct primes $p, q, r$. A number $n \ge 2$ is "triple-prime-compliant" if there exist three distinct primes $p, q, r$ such that:

Whenever $a_1, \dots, a_n$ are $n$ distinct positive integers such that for every pair $j < k$, at least one of $p, q, r$ divides $a_j - a_k$, then at least one of $p, q, r$ divides all $\binom{n}{2}$ differences.

- But no single prime divides all differences
